headline: Monhegan holds, Egg Rock feeds, and Penobscot cod stay down deep
subhead: Late-August stability across Midcoast Maine keeps stripers at the river mouths and groundfish tucked into the Bay's cold channels.
body_markdown:
Forty years of hauling gear out of Boothbay teaches you one thing about the last week of August: the water doesn't rush anything. Cod don't leave the bottom just because the calendar flips, and stripers don't quit a river mouth until the water tells them to. Back in the '90s there was a stretch of Augusts just like this one — flat, steady, boring on paper — that turned into some of the best September fishing this coast has seen once the nights cooled and the bait got nervous. That's the pattern setting up again.

We called this one last week — flagged stable, typical late-August conditions holding through the next 72 hours, and that's exactly what the fleet found. No abrupt shift, no warm-water stress pushing fish around like it's doing to waters south of here. Penobscot Bay and the outer islands have stayed clean and comfortable, water color holding good and green rather than milky, and that steadiness is why the bite, while not explosive, has been dependable enough to plan a trip around.

Striped bass are still working the river mouths — Kennebec off Popham, the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta, and the Georges River mouth down at Port Clyde. The pattern hasn't changed much in three weeks: fish stack on the last two hours of the ebb where warm river water dumps into the cooler bay, and bait — pogies and small herring — gets pinned against the current seam. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, three-quarter to one ounce, worked slow along bottom structure, have taken slot fish to 30 inches. Live mackerel under a slip float, drifted right on that seam, is still the more consistent producer for the bigger fish holding deeper in the channel. Eastern Egg Rock continues to hold bass around the ledges on the up-tide side, particularly on the last of the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the rock — small poppers early, then switch to soft plastics once the sun's up and the fish stop showing on top.

Monhegan is fishing true to form for this time of year. Pollock are up on the surface working bait schools at first light and again toward dusk, and anyone with a light spinning rod and a two-ounce diamond jig has been getting into them steady off the eastern ledges. Cod are holding deeper, 60 to 90 feet on the northwest side where the bottom drops off hard — jigging with a heavier diamond jig or a bait rig tipped with clam has produced fish in the 6 to 12 pound range, nothing to write home about but enough to keep interest up. The groundfish bite off Monhegan tends to hold through September before the fish slide deeper, so there's time yet.

Inside the Bay, the deeper channels between Islesboro and Vinalhaven, and the water off Stonington toward Isle au Haut, are still carrying cod and some haddock, though the haddock have thinned out compared to July. Boats working those channels are marking fish 80 to 110 feet down on structure — ledge edges and the old lobster-ground humps that every captain up here has scratched into a chart at some point. Jigging is out-producing bait rigs right now; a 6-ounce diamond or a Norwegian-style jig worked with a short, sharp lift-and-drop has been the difference-maker.

Mackerel remain the one truly reliable bite in the zone — schools have been thick off Boothbay Harbor's town landing and around Rockland breakwater, taking mackerel trees on light tackle with almost no effort. That abundance is exactly what's keeping the bass and pollock fed and staged where they are; when the mackerel move, everything else follows. Bluefish have made scattered appearances in the warmer pockets around Casco Bay's edge and into outer Boothbay waters, nothing like the numbers being seen to the south, but worth a cast if you're marking bait and see slashing on top.

Looking at the next several days, expect more of the same — no big weather disruption on the immediate horizon, tides building modestly toward the coming moon, which should tighten up the current seams at the river mouths and sharpen the bite window on the ebb. If there's only one day to fish this week, first light at a river mouth on the last two hours of the outgoing tide is the safer bet for stripers, with Monhegan's dawn pollock bite as a strong second option if the wind stays light enough to make the run out. The Bay's groundfish will keep holding deep and steady; no reason to expect a sudden change there until the water starts its real cool-down in a few weeks, which is when the cod tend to push shallower and get considerably easier to find.
